newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Fed official's speech eyed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Fed official's speech eyed.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities faced another dull trading session Wednesday as market participants had little to focus on other than a policymaker's speech.
William McDonough, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee, was slated to speak at 830EST/1330GMT.
Producer price data were set for Thursday release and Friday will see crucial monthly nonfarm payrolls report. And, lacking a shock to the market, analysts expected trading volume to be very light.
"Unless energy prices or commodities as a whole really take off, we should trade in a very tight range," a trader said.
There reportedly was hedge fund selling of 10- and 30-year Treasuries on Tuesday and should more of this activity occur, it may hurt the market on Wednesday.

Another negative for the market this week has been a decline in the value of the U.S. dollar against the Japanese yen. The dollar has tumbled in recent days as Japanese finance officials have issued statements that indicated the government does not want to see excessive yen weakness.

"Guys rooting for the market to go down will use their positions and theories to try to bid it down," said Richard Schwarz, economist at Zions First National Bank. However, Schwarz said he wasn't sure dollar movements would have a strong effect on Treasuries.
He said Wednesday most likely will be a very uneventful session.
"We probably saw most of the action that we're going to before the release of PPI," said Richard Gilhooly, trading strategist at Paribas Capital Markets. "Most people are already positioned."
Concern was building that the FOMC might vote to tighten interest rates when it next meets on Feb. 4 and 5, although most economists do not expect such a move until the March meeting.
Still, Alan Levenson, economist at UBS Securities, said the tenor of comments coming from Fed officials has been tranquil of late.

"It should be a quiet session and we'll be biding our time with everyone else," Levenson said. He said upward revisions on Friday's employment report may be considered by some in the Wall Street dealer community.
In late trading Tuesday the 30-year bond was down 6/32 at 99-10/32 to yield 6.79 percent.

The two-year note was at 99-19/32 to yield 5.97 percent, unchanged. The five-year note was unchanged at 99-9/32 to yield 6.29 percent, while the 10-year note was at 99-21/32, down 2/32, to yield 6.55 percent.
Federal funds closed at 5-13/16, near the Federal Reserve's current target level of 5.25 percent and were expected to open trade Wednesday between 5-3/16 percent.
